```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

When parallel trends holds only conditional on covariates, researchers often
add the covariates to a TWFE regression. Caetano and Callaway (2024) show
that the TWFE coefficient can then be written as a reweighting estimator:
a weighted comparison of changes in outcomes between treated and untreated
units. The implicit weights balance the covariates that enter the regression
in the form they enter it (for example, the change in a time-varying
covariate), but not other functions of them, such as their levels. If
parallel trends depends on covariates that the weights do not balance, the
TWFE estimate can be biased even when treatment effects are the same for
everyone.

This suggests a diagnostic: compute the implicit weights and check how well
they balance the covariates that parallel trends is thought to depend on.
The same diagnostic applies to augmented inverse probability weighting
(AIPW) and regression adjustment, whose implicit weights balance every
covariate in the outcome model.

The example follows the application in Caetano and Callaway (2024): the
effect of stand-your-ground laws on homicides (Cheng and Hoekstra, 2013),
using a state-level panel for 2000-2010 from the `causaldata` package.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(twfeweights)
data(castle, package = "causaldata")
castle <- as.data.frame(castle)
```

## Two periods

With two periods, take 2000 (before any state adopted a law) and 2010. The
group variable is 0 for states that had not adopted by 2010 and 2010 for
those that had.

```{r}
castle2 <- subset(castle, year %in% c(2000, 2010))
castle2$G <- BMisc::get_group(castle2, "sid", tname = "year", treatname = "post")
```

### TWFE regression

With two periods, a TWFE regression with time-varying covariates is a
regression of the change in log homicides on the treatment indicator and
the change in the covariates. `two_period_reg_weights()` returns its
coefficient, the implicit weights and a balance table:

```{r}
tw <- two_period_reg_weights(
  yname = "l_homicide", tname = "year", idname = "sid", gname = "G",
  xformula = ~ l_police + unemployrt, data = castle2
)
tw$est
tw$cov_balance_df[, c("covariate", "unweighted_diff", "weighted_diff")]
```

The first row is the outcome; its weighted difference is the TWFE estimate.
The weights balance the *changes* in police and unemployment exactly, but
the 2000 *levels* stay about as unbalanced as before weighting. If trends in
homicides depend on the level of these covariates, TWFE does not adjust for
it. `ggtwfeweights()` plots standardized differences (differences divided by
the pooled standard deviation, see `pooled_sd()`):

```{r}
ggtwfeweights(tw)
```

### AIPW and regression adjustment

`two_period_aipw_weights()` does the same for AIPW. The outcome model below
includes the 2000 levels of both covariates and the change in police;
setting `pscore_formula = ~1` and `pscore_d_covs_formula = ~1` (no
covariates in the propensity score) gives regression adjustment.

```{r}
ra <- two_period_aipw_weights(
  yname = "l_homicide", tname = "year", idname = "sid", gname = "G",
  xformula = ~ l_police + unemployrt, d_covs_formula = ~l_police,
  pscore_formula = ~1, pscore_d_covs_formula = ~1, data = castle2
)
ra$est
ra$cov_balance_df[, c("covariate", "unweighted_diff", "weighted_diff")]
```

Every covariate in the outcome model is balanced exactly, in levels and in
changes. The `weightsname` argument adds sampling weights, and
`extra_balance_vars_formula` reports balance for covariates that are not in
the model.

```{r}
ggtwfeweights(ra)
```

Two further diagnostics are worth reporting alongside balance. The
`ess` element is the effective sample size of the comparison group under
the implicit weights (see `effective_sample_size()`): the more the weights
are concentrated on a few units, the smaller it is. And
`ggtwfeweights(..., plot_relative_to_target = TRUE)` shows whether the
weights also move the treated group away from its own covariate
distribution.

## Staggered adoption

States adopted stand-your-ground laws in different years, so the full panel
has staggered adoption. The group variable is now the first year a state is
treated (0 if never treated in the sample).

```{r}
castle$G <- BMisc::get_group(castle, "sid", tname = "year", treatname = "post")
table(castle$G[castle$year == 2000])
```

### TWFE regression

`implicit_twfe_weights()` decomposes the TWFE coefficient into weighted
comparisons between each treated group and the never-treated group in each
year. With `base_period = "gmin1"`, each comparison uses the year before the
group was first treated as its base period, as in `did::att_gt()`.

```{r}
twm <- implicit_twfe_weights(
  yname = "l_homicide", tname = "year", idname = "sid", gname = "G",
  xformula = ~ l_police + unemployrt, base_period = "gmin1", data = castle
)
twm$est
coef(fixest::feols(l_homicide ~ post + l_police + unemployrt | sid + year,
  data = castle
))["post"]
```

`summary()` splits the estimate. `alpha post only` is the part that comes
from post-treatment comparisons; `pta violations bias` is the part that
comes from pre-treatment comparisons, which should be close to zero if
parallel trends holds before treatment. Here most of the TWFE estimate comes
from pre-treatment comparisons.

```{r}
s <- summary(twm)
```

`twfe_cov_bal()` adds balance statistics for any covariates, which are
averaged over time within each state first. The summary and plot average
them over post-treatment cells:

```{r}
twm <- twfe_cov_bal(twm, ~ l_police + unemployrt + poverty + l_income)
ggtwfeweights(twm)
```

### Regression adjustment

`implicit_aipw_weights()` estimates the overall average treatment effect on
the treated, $ATT^o$, by AIPW or regression adjustment for each group and
post-treatment year, and combines them as in Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021).
With few states in each timing group, the propensity score is hard to
estimate, so regression adjustment is a natural choice here. Covariates in
`xformula` enter through their level in the base period ($g-1$), as in
`did::att_gt()`; `d_covs_formula` adds their change since the base period.

```{r}
ram <- implicit_aipw_weights(
  yname = "l_homicide", tname = "year", idname = "sid", gname = "G",
  xformula = ~ l_police + unemployrt, d_covs_formula = ~ l_police + unemployrt,
  pscore_formula = ~1, pscore_d_covs_formula = ~1, data = castle
)
ram$est
```

Without `d_covs_formula`, the estimate equals `did::att_gt()` with the same
covariates and `est_method = "reg"`, aggregated with
`did::aggte(type = "group")`.

```{r}
ram <- aipw_cov_bal(ram, ~ l_police + unemployrt + poverty + l_income)
ggtwfeweights(ram)
```

Comparing the two balance plots shows which covariates each estimator
balances, and how well. The same comparison with other covariates, in the
outcome model or only in the balance check, is a way to see how sensitive
the estimate is to how covariates enter.

## References

Caetano, Carolina and Brantly Callaway. "Difference-in-Differences when
Parallel Trends Holds Conditional on Covariates." Working paper (2024).
arXiv:2406.15288.

Callaway, Brantly and Pedro H. C. Sant'Anna. "Difference-in-Differences with
Multiple Time Periods." *Journal of Econometrics* 225.2 (2021): 200-230.

Cheng, Cheng and Mark Hoekstra. "Does Strengthening Self-Defense Law Deter
Crime or Escalate Violence? Evidence from Expansions to Castle Doctrine."
*Journal of Human Resources* 48.3 (2013): 821-854.
